newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.S. plane seeks "missing" refugees in east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.S. plane seeks "missing" refugees in east Zaire.

text.p: A U.S. intelligence-gathering aircraft circled above the eastern Zairean towns of Goma and Sake on Tuesday as the hunt went on for hundreds of thousands of "missing" Rwandan refugees.
"We are back to where we were two weeks ago," said UNHCR spokesman Ray Wilkinson in Goma. "Where are the refugees? It's hide-and-seek. Now you see them, now you don't."
The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees estimated there were 1.2 million Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire until mid-November.
But on November 15, many decided to return home to escape intense fighting in the area between the Zairean army, Zairean rebels and Hutu militiamen.
Aid agencies and the U.S. military estimate that up to 600,000 have returned to Rwanda, but where the rest are remains a mystery.
"We had reports yesterday that a large group was moving up the edge of the lake (Kivu), but now we are hearing that the road is clear," Wilkinson said.
According to various reports, thousands of Rwandan refugees from camps around Bukavu south of Lake Kivu are moving north towards the small town of Sake, north of the lake.

Anything up to 300,000 Rwandan refugees from the camps of Katale, Kahindo and Kibumba are thought to be hiding in forests and bush in a huge 5,000-square-km (2,000-square-mile) area from Rutshuru in the north to Numbi in the south.

"In the last two days we have had 1,400 refugees from Bukavu who have arrived in Sake, and come back to Rwanda via Goma, but now, perhaps because of fighting, those in Sake might have taken to the hills," Wilkinson said.
"All these refugees came from Numbi, en route from Bukavu, where they had been turned off the road," he added.
The U.S. Navy P3 Orion reconnaissance aircraft, designed to hunt submarines, circled for more than two hours over the area.
Other planes flying the area recently have attracted rebel fire, but the U.S. plane was not fired upon.
Access to Sake, 20 kms (12 miles) west of Goma, was again denied to journalists and foreign aid workers by rebel troops, although local cars and minibuses were allowed in.
Aid workers had to quit the area because of the fighting and the rebels have not allowed them in since, although they agreed this week to allow assessment work to begin.
Local aid workers, refugees and villagers confirm that there has been fighting south of Sake, towards Minova, for the last two days.

Aid sources said an unconfirmed number of officials from the Mai Mai ethnic group died on Monday in an ambush involving landmines and anti-tank mines between Sake and Kirotshe, 10 km (six miles) to the south.
